header:
Date: 2026-05-14
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jared Cole (Zenexus CTO), Maya Ortiz (Zenexus Head of ML), Samir Patel (Zenexus Staff Engineer)
summary: Redwood hosted API demo focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, key generation parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/idempotency patterns, and how Console/Optimize features help control cost and latency. Customer is evaluating for a POC to power in-product assistant with strict latency and data residency questions; next steps: pricing & SLA, benchmark template, POC kickoff.
topics: Parameters: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences
Latency vs cost tradeoffs; hosted vs dedicated vs private
transcript:
00:00 Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Alex, AE at Redwood. We've got priya from SE with me. how's everyone doing?
00:06 Jared Cole: Good thanks, Jared here. hey Priya.
00:09 Priya Nair: Hi Jared, Maya, Samir. excited to walk through the hosted API and show streaming and some tips.
00:15 Maya Ortiz: Great, we only have about 50 minutes so maybe hit the high points, we're most curious about latency, cost and data handling.
00:22 Alex Kim: Perfect. quick agenda: 1) show live chat demo with streaming, 2) go over request params and retries, 3) point out console and optimize features, 4) Q&A and next steps. sound good?
00:30 Samir Patel: Sounds good. we run real-time suggestions inside our product, target p95 under 300ms for short responses. is that realistic on hosted?
00:38 Priya Nair: short answer - yes for many models, depending on payload and concurrency. longer answer - there are tradeoffs. hosted API has optimized kernels and continuous batching, but latency depends on model choice, token length, and batching policy.
00:52 Alex Kim: i'll kick off the demo, i'm going to call the chat endpoint, show streaming chunks. you'll see partial tokens as they arrive.
00:58 (screen share starts)
01:01 Priya Nair: okay i'm sending a chat message to the hosted endpoint with model redwood-large-v1 (demo model). param set: temperature 0.2, max_tokens 120, top_p 0.95, stream true. note: we set an idempotency key per user request.
01:15 (tiny pause)
01:18 Priya Nair: streaming started - chunk 1: "Sure -" chunk 2: " I can help with that. For your product, would you like a short summary or an action plan?"
01:30 Maya Ortiz: oh that's neat, i like the partial rendering. how do you handle reconnects if the client drops mid-stream?
01:35 Priya Nair: good Q. for reconnects we recommend using a resume token approach for long-form streaming. for shorter chats the client should retry with same idempotency key and the server will return the finished response if it completed; if not completed, the request is retried with backoff. we also expose status endpoints to check final status in case of flakey net. sometimes transcription shows 'status codes uhh' - we return 2xx for success, 429 for rate limits, 5xx transient, and 410 for non-retryable.
02:05 Samir Patel: do you enforce any hard rate limits per API key? we have bursts up to 200 req/s.
02:10 Alex Kim: hosted does enforce tiered rate limits and we can white-list burst windows for early customers. for sustained high throughput we'd suggest dedicated capacity.
02:18 Jared Cole: what about retries - are we supposed to implement exponential backoff on our side? and what about idempotency and duplicate tokens risk?
02:26 Priya Nair: yes implement client-side exponential backoff with jitter. Redwood supports idempotency keys - if you retry with the same key, we dedupe and return same response when possible. for streaming you may need to handle partial receipts, so we recommend pausing the UI while trying recovery flows.
02:42 Maya Ortiz: any guidance on parameters - like we see cheaper but flickery output with temperature 0.9, and too generic at 0.0. what's recommended for assistant responses?
02:51 Priya Nair: for assistant/FAQ style we recommend temp 0.0-0.3 and top_p around 0.9-0.95. keep max_tokens tight - you pay per token - and use stop sequences for structured outputs. also use logprobs for sampling analysis in POC.
03:08 Alex Kim: want to touch on cost controls - Console gives per-route token breakdown and you can set quotas. Redwood Optimize also suggests batching and quantization options by workload.
03:19 Jared Cole: quick ques on model variants - can you pin model versions and fall back to smaller models automatically? we have spikes where cost balloons.
03:26 Priya Nair: yes, model pinning and rollout policies are in Console. you can configure smart routing policies: route by latency, cost, or region. fallback to a compatible smaller/quantized model when capacity or cost thresholds hit.
03:40 Samir Patel: about security: does hosted keep request logs? we need SOC 2, SAML SSO, and KMS for keying. also data residency - EU vs US.
03:48 Alex Kim: hosted offers SOC 2 compliant logging and RBAC; SSO via SAML/Okta; we integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest on Private and Dedicated, hosted has managed KMS but we provide audit logs and DLP controls. we also have region selections for EU and US to help with residency.
04:05 Maya Ortiz: any chance of on-prem or VPC? some of our customers force us to have VPC endpoints.
04:08 Priya Nair: yep - Redwood Private supports customer-managed VPCs and on-prem packaging for air-gapped environments. for the POC, hosted is fastest; dedicated or private can come later for stricter controls.
04:20 Jared Cole: nice. can you talk a bit about caching? our assistant often repeats the same prefix for multiple similar prompts.
04:26 Priya Nair: we support prefix/KV caching and partial response caching. in practice you can cache at the prefix level to avoid re-computing tokens. Console exposes cache hit/miss metrics so you can tune TTLs. this reduces unit cost dramatically for high reuse prompts.
04:42 Samir Patel: do you do continuous batching on hosted? sometimes batching adds latency.
04:46 Priya Nair: yes continuous batching is used but tuned by latency SLOs; we have per-tenant batching windows and you can set latency SLOs to favor lower p95s at expense of less batching. Redwood Optimize will suggest batch sizes and quantization profiles to balance cost.
05:00 Maya Ortiz: can we run a quick benchmark example? we want to see p50/p95 on a 20 token response.
05:05 Priya Nair: sure - i'll run a small script from the quickstart repo. note: this is a demo env, numbers are illustrative.
05:12 (short pause)
05:18 Priya Nair: running 100 requests, concurrency 10, model redwood-medium-v1, temperature 0.2, stream disabled for latency measure. result: p50 ~ 120ms, p95 ~ 280ms in this region; token length ~ 20. your mileage may vary depending on exact model and region.
05:34 Jared Cole: that's promising. our in-app path needs p95 < 300ms for short replies, so that looks doable.
05:40 Alex Kim: for cost estimates, we'll provide a cost model sheet. also note quantized variants reduce cost and memory but can slightly change output quality - Redwood Optimize simulates and scores quality tradeoffs for you.
05:56 Maya Ortiz: about retries and dedupe - if a retry happens and the server ends up producing a slightly different tokenization, do we get consistent completions?
06:03 Priya Nair: with the same idempotency key we aim for deterministic returned final result when possible; nondeterminism can come from nondeterministic model sampling unless you set low temp or deterministic decode. for deterministic behavior, pin temp=0 and use nucleus/top_p tuned appropriately or use greedy decoding.
06:22 Samir Patel: what about embedding endpoints and separate rate quotas? we use embeddings for search in another service so want to ensure the hosted plan covers both.
06:29 Alex Kim: embeddings are separate units with their own pricing; Console shows combined spend and per-endpoint quotas so you can control them.
06:37 Jared Cole: any gotchas with streaming on mobile - we have flaky 4G connections.
06:42 Priya Nair: resume strategies: short lived responses - best to retry and fetch final result with idempotency; long streams - include sequence numbers in chunks and a resume token. also use optimistic UI updates. if connectivity is expected to be poor, returning shorter summarized responses helps.
06:58 Maya Ortiz: ok good. i want to go deeper on SDKs - do you provide official clients? language support?
07:03 Alex Kim: yes official SDKs for JS, Python, and a lightweight mobile HTTP pattern. we also have example streaming clients in the quickstart repo.
07:12 Samir Patel: can we run POC on our integration tests? like we want to run smoke tests against the API every build.
07:18 Priya Nair: yes, we often provision short-lived API tokens for CI, and you can set low quotas. for POCs we give sandbox credits.
07:25 Jared Cole: technical deep dive question - can you explain kernel selection and quantization briefly? we have an infra person who's curious.
07:31 Priya Nair: sure - the runtime chooses kernels based on model architecture, seq length distribution and hardware. quantization profiles reduce numeric precision for weights, e.g., int8 or 4-bit, reducing mem and cost. Redwood's profile picks kernels compatible with quantized execution to keep perf. quantized models are validated so we flag quality regression risks in Optimize.
07:56 Maya Ortiz: any references or docs for SOC 2 and security architecture?
08:00 Alex Kim: we'll share the security playbook and SOC 2 report under NDA. also we'll include our network diagram and KMS integration notes.
08:10 Samir Patel: what's the typical timeline to start a POC and then move to Dedicated?
08:14 Alex Kim: POC can start within a week - sandbox + benchmark script. moving to Dedicated is a few weeks to provision capacity - depends on commit size. Private/VPC takes longer due to network config.
08:25 Maya Ortiz: ok let's talk about decision criteria - for us it's latency, cost per convo, and data handling. we need a clear way to measure regressions.
08:33 Priya Nair: we recommend a small eval suite: fixed prompt set, quality metrics (ROUGE, human eval on samples), latency buckets, and cost per 1k tokens. Console allows alerting on quality regression if you upload evals; Optimize ties changes to rollout.
08:50 Jared Cole: competitors we looked at - openai is simplest, Anthropic for safety, Vertex for cloud integration. how do you position Redwood vs those?
08:59 Alex Kim: Redwood focuses on production-grade serving and ops controls: unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, advanced batching/caching, transparent per-token economics, and rollout tools. we partner with cloud infra but provide a consistent surface so you don't rebuild serving.
09:15 Maya Ortiz: makes sense. couple quick followups: 1) can you whitepaper batching parameters? 2) sample streaming client for android? 3) SOC2 docs?
09:25 Alex Kim: yes to all - i'll send the docs and priya will attach the repo.
09:30 (wrap up)
09:31 Alex Kim: recap: we'll send pricing & SLA, security docs, benchmark template + quickstart, and schedule POC kickoff. action items recorded. any other Qs?
09:40 Maya Ortiz: none right now. thanks - we'll review and get back on dates.
09:44 Jared Cole: thanks everyone.
09:46 Priya Nair: thanks all - chat in slack.
09:50 (call ends)
notes: Demo used model 'redwood-large-v1' and 'redwood-medium-v1' as examples; actual tenant may use different variants.
Priya demonstrated streaming chunks and explained idempotency and retry best-practices.
Benchmarks shown were illustrative; Redwood to provide formal benchmark template and run with customer's dataset for POC.
